title: Shortest Slice to Sort
statement:
Given an integer array nums, find the shortest contiguous slice such that sorting just that slice in ascending order leaves the whole array sorted in ascending order. Return its length.

If the array is already sorted, return 0. Equal neighbours count as sorted.

examples.why: Sort [7, 4, 5] into [4, 5, 7] and the array is in order. The 1, 3 and 9 are already in place.
Already sorted, and the repeated 2 is fine.
The only drop is 6 → 2, but sorting just [6, 2] gives 1, 4, 2, 6, …. The 2 belongs before the 4, so the slice is [4, 6, 2].

hints: Compare the array with a sorted copy of itself. Which positions differ?
Can you find the boundaries without sorting? An element is out of place if something to its left is bigger, or something to its right is smaller.
Scan left to right with a running max: the last index whose value is below the running max is the right end. Scan right to left with a running min for the left end.

explain.intuition:
The slice must cover every element that is not already in its final position. Sorting a copy and comparing shows exactly those positions: the first and last mismatch are the slice ends. That costs O(n log n).

Without sorting: an element is fine on its right side only if nothing before it is larger. Walk left to right keeping the running maximum; every time a value is smaller than that maximum, it must move, so it extends the right end. Mirror it from the right with a running minimum to find the left end. The two walks automatically pull in the extra neighbours, like the 4 in example 3, that a "find the first drop" scan misses.
steps: Walk i from left to right with maxSeen. If nums[i] < maxSeen, set end = i; else update maxSeen.
Walk i from right to left with minSeen. If nums[i] > minSeen, set start = i; else update minSeen.
pitfalls: Using only the first and last descent. In [1, 4, 6, 2, 7, 8] that gives 2; the 2 must travel past the 4.
Treating equal values as out of order. Use strict comparisons so [1, 2, 2, 3] returns 0.
Returning 1 for a sorted array because end − start + 1 is computed from default values. Handle the sorted case first.

solutions.title: Compare with a sorted copy
solutions.idea: The first and last positions where the array differs from its sorted version bound the slice.

solutions.title: Running max from the left, running min from the right
solutions.idea: Anything below the max before it must move, which fixes the right end; anything above the min after it must move, which fixes the left end.

followups: Return the slice boundaries instead of the length.
Instead of sorting one slice, you may sort several disjoint slices. What is the most pieces you can split the array into so that sorting each piece sorts the whole?
